summary: Redwood AE+SE ran a structured output and function-calling demo for Meridian Retail focused on JSON mode, schema validation, and guardrails. Meridian is evaluating for customer support automation and product merchandising recommendations; they requested POC benchmarks, security docs and a follow-up infra call.
topics: Security & deployment options (Hosted vs Dedicated vs VPC)
transcript:
[00:00] Jamie Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Jamie with Redwood, AE on the account, with Ravi our Solutions Eng. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Priya Desai: Good, thanks. We have about 45 minutes, want to see the structured output stuff and understand guardrails — and we have a couple infra people after this.
[00:14] Jamie Chen: Perfect. Quick agenda: show JSON mode / schema enforcement, function calling for downstream tools, show Console Optimize suggestions, then Q&A and next steps. Ravi, want to kick off?
[00:22] Ravi Patel: Yep. I'll share my screen — minor note, audio might be fuzzy, lemme know. So the use case Meridian mentioned — automated product merchandising rules and customer support categorization — is a great fit. We'll demo generating structured JSON that maps to your downstream systems and then call a mock API to show tool-calling.
[00:38] Laura Kim: Quick context: we currently call OpenAI for completions, but the results are inconsistent and we do heavy post-processing. Latency matters for live chat, cost matters for bulk merchandising runs. Also security: we need SOC2 plus KMS for keys, and we usually prefer VPC when PII is in scope.
[00:56] Ravi Patel: Totally. We'll show both hosted and dedicated fallbacks; Redwood supports private VPC and KMS integrations, and audit logs for every request. For the demo I'll use a curated open model we validated for latency.
[01:12] Jamie Chen: Note — we also have Optimize recommendations that will suggest batching and quantization for offline workloads to reduce unit cost while retaining quality.
[01:20] Ravi Patel: Alright jumping into the JSON mode. You'll see a schema on the side — required fields: intent, confidence, entities (list), routing. We instruct the model to emit strict JSON and Redwood applies schema validation and sanitization.
[01:35] [screenshare noise] 
[01:45] Ravi Patel: Example prompt: generate a ticket classification JSON. I'll run it live.
[01:52] System: (transcription error) the first attempt had a stray comma and the model emitted a trailing comma — Redwood's sanitizer flagged it and we apply post-parse hooks.
[02:05] Ravi Patel: So here's the tool-calling piece: the model can return a structured 'call' object that references a function name and arguments. Redwood can map that to an HTTP webhook or internal tool. I'll trigger a mock 'create_ticket' function — notice the payload is validated against the function schema before the call.
[02:22] Laura Kim: If the model outputs malformed args, can you reject the call?
[02:26] Ravi Patel: Yes — we have guardrails. The runtime checks schema and type, and if it fails, we can either return an error to the client or fallback to a safe handler. You can also enable human-in-the-loop for high risk domains.
[02:36] Sam Torres: How do you store audit logs? We need per-token traceability and the ability to pull logs for an ID.
[02:42] Jamie Chen: Audit logs are stored in customer-shippable logs and can be forwarded to your SIEM or to S3. Each request has a unique trace ID, with token counts and latency breakdowns. For private deployments we support in-region storage and customer-managed KMS.
[02:56] Ravi Patel: Back to the demo — I'll flip to the Console. This is the per-route dashboard; you can see schema failure rates, sample outputs, and Optimize suggestions. For example, the console suggests enabling prefix caching for repeated user prompts in chat to cut tokens.
[03:15] [pause] 
[03:20] Priya Desai: For POC we want to run two models: one quantized and cheap, one FP16 for latency-sensitive chat. Can Redwood run both and route based on latency budget?
[03:30] Ravi Patel: Yep, smart routing can send low-latency requests to the fast path model and cheaper batch jobs to the quantized variant. You can pin rollout percentages too — like 10% to the new model.
[03:44] Laura Kim: What's the SLA on dedicated? We want 99.9 for latency and uptime ideally.
[03:49] Jamie Chen: Dedicated includes SLA-backed uptime and reserved GPU pools. We can size the pool based on throughput targets; I'll include our SLA doc in the follow-up.
[03:58] Sam Torres: Network wise, do you allow customer IP allowlists and SAML SSO for access?
[04:03] Ravi Patel: Yes to both. For Private we do VPC peering, security groups, and you can plug in SAML, RBAC and detailed audit logs.
[04:10] [transcription artifact — 'VPC' heard as 'VPCP']
[04:15] Jamie Chen: Quick aside on costs — we'll share a calculator. Optimize can recommend batching window sizes; for example, 50ms batching for chat vs 500ms for background runs. That saves tokens and gpu time.
[04:30] Ravi Patel: Now I'll show function calling with a slightly more complex schema — nested objects for product recommendation: product_id, score, reasons[], recommended_action {type, target}. The schema prevents extra fields and enforces types.
[04:46] Ravi Patel: Running it… model returns call: {name: "upsert_recommendation", args: {...}}. The runtime validates then executes HTTP POST to a mock endpoint. You can see the Console showing the request and the function response.
[05:02] Laura Kim: If the model hallucinates a product_id that doesn't exist, can we cross-check against our catalog?
[05:07] Ravi Patel: Absolutely — you can wire pre-call validators that query your catalog. If mismatched, either reject or map to closest candidate. For high-sensitivity data you can also run a dry-run where the model output is captured but not executed.
[05:22] Priya Desai: For the POC, we also need to prove compliance — can we get your SOC 2 and pen test reports?
[05:28] Jamie Chen: Yes — we'll attach SOC 2 and ISO artifacts. We also provide architecture diagrams for Private deployments and details on KMS integration.
[05:36] Sam Torres: About latency testing — can you run a benchmark from our region?
[05:40] Ravi Patel: We'll spin a benchmark from our dedicated region closest to you; for Private we can run on-prem benchmarks too. I'll put together a config with concurrency, sequence lengths, and cold vs warm cache.
[05:51] [short crosstalk] 
[05:54] Ravi Patel: One more note on guardrails: Redwood supports function-level allowlists and per-route RBAC so only certain clients can invoke sensitive functions. Also rate limiting to avoid downstream overcall.
[06:09] Laura Kim: Regarding data retention — can we set retention to zero for certain routes?
[06:12] Jamie Chen: Yes. Hosted routes can be configured to not retain logs; Private gives you full control. We'll include the retention settings doc.
[06:21] Priya Desai: Ok, next steps then?
[06:24] Jamie Chen: Recap: we'll send pricing + SLA, run an initial benchmark (Ravi), Meridian provides sample data, and we'll schedule infra/security deep dive. Also we'll propose Dedicated sizing and POC timeline.
[06:38] Sam Torres: Sounds good. If you can include cost estimates for both hosted burst and reserved dedicated, that helps.
[06:44] Jamie Chen: Will do. Thanks all, we'll follow up in email with the attachments.
[06:50] [00:06:50] Meeting ends — approximate transcript length aligned with 48 minutes call (transcript clipped for brevity)
notes: Demo showed JSON mode + function-calling mapped to webhook with schema validation
